title: Coastline Ruler Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you measure a coastline with shorter and shorter rulers, watch its length keep growing, then read off how wiggly it is.
pitch: You walk a ruler along a wiggly coast, shrink it, and see the length climb instead of settling, while a circle quietly settles to a fixed answer. A live chart of ruler size against measured length turns the climb into a straight line whose steepness is the coast's roughness (its fractal dimension), and you finish by ranking mystery coasts by eye and checking yourself.
firstMinute: The first frame shows a jagged generated coast with a ruler already walking along it in steps, a length readout, and a slider labelled 'ruler size'. Dragging the slider down makes the ruler re-walk the coast and the length number climb, with a second panel beside it where a smooth circle barely changes. First success: the visitor sees the same coast give a bigger length just by choosing a smaller ruler.
conceptsToLearn: Length can be estimated by counting how many equal ruler steps it takes to walk along a curve
whyNow: Timeless and very visual: it makes the coastline paradox a thing you do rather than a fact you read, and ends on a number (roughness) the visitor can measure themselves. It is a geometry lesson, not number theory, so it sits apart from the other maths candidates this round.

purposeDetail.concept: A wiggly curve such as a coastline has no single length: the measured length depends on the ruler. For a curve with fractal dimension D between 1 and 2, the measured length grows roughly like (ruler size) raised to the power (1 minus D) as the ruler shrinks, so a log-log plot of length against ruler size is close to a straight line with slope 1 minus D (a plot of the step count instead has slope minus D, so the page says which one it draws). A smooth curve has D = 1 and its length settles; the Koch curve has D = ln 4 / ln 3, about 1.26.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: The coastline paradox is usually quoted as a fun fact and stops there. Few explanations let the learner do the measuring, see why the line on the log-log plot appears, and use its slope to get a number.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults and students aged about 14 and up, teachers, and anyone who has met 'fractals' as pretty pictures only.
misconceptions: A coastline has one true length that a good enough measurement would find
A smaller ruler just gives a more accurate number of the same quantity, so the length must level off for every curve
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: On the log-log chart the points for the Koch coast fall on a straight line while the circle's line is flat, and the steepness of the coast's line is exactly the extra wiggliness the ruler keeps discovering.
demos: Rung 1: walk a ruler along a gentle curve and a circle; the length settles as the ruler shrinks
Rung 2: the same ruler on a jagged coast; the length keeps climbing and the visitor predicts the next value before it appears
Rung 3: build a Koch coast step by step and watch each stage multiply the length by four thirds while the ruler shrinks by a third
Rung 4: the live log-log chart appears and the visitor drags a fitted line through the points to read the slope
Rung 5: turn the slope into a dimension and compare the circle (1), the Koch coast (about 1.26), and a seeded random coast whose roughness the visitor guesses first
Rung 6: a 'zoom out, zoom in' toggle shows a real quoted example (Great Britain at two ruler sizes) with the figures labelled as quoted, not measured here
checkQuestions: If halving the ruler makes a coast's measured length grow by about 10 percent, is the coast smoother or rougher than the Koch coast (where halving grows it by about 20 percent)?
Why does a circle's measured length stop changing while a jagged coast's does not?
Why is a log-log chart, not an ordinary chart, the right one here?
Can a curve have dimension 1.5? What would that say about it?

research.summary: Re-checked by search: the Great Britain figures (about 2,800 km with 100 km units, about 3,400 km with 50 km units; one popular site says about 3,500) appear in an encyclopedia article and a blog; Richardson's relation, length proportional to step size to the power 1 minus D, and the straight line on log-log axes appear in a maths blog, a spatial-analysis tutorial and MathWorld; Koch curve length growth by 4/3 and dimension ln 4 / ln 3 (about 1.2619) appear in several explainers and follow from arithmetic. The figure D about 1.25 for the west coast of Britain comes from Richardson's divider data as listed on a university fractals page and repeated in two other results; modern re-fits give lower values (about 1.15 to 1.21 in one tutorial, depending on its version). Real coasts are straight on the plot only over a limited range of scales, and a 2006 paper reports numerical artefacts of the divider method even on the Koch island, so the page must say 'close to' and not 'equal to'.

facts.claim: Measuring the coast of Great Britain with 100 km units gives about 2,800 km and with 50 km units about 3,400 km (one popular site says about 3,500 km); a coastline has no well-defined length.
The Koch curve has dimension ln 4 / ln 3, about 1.2619, and its length grows by a factor of 4/3 at each stage so it is unbounded.

Richardson's relation: measured length is about a constant times (step size) to the power (1 minus D), so length against step size is a straight line on log-log axes with slope 1 minus D; the dimension of a coast lies between 1 and 2.

A coastline's measured length depends on the ruler, and a smaller ruler gives a longer result; the effect was studied by Richardson, then in Mandelbrot's 1967 paper 'How long is the coast of Britain?'.

Richardson's divider data give D of about 1.25 for the west coast of Britain, a figure Mandelbrot also quoted; a modern re-fit in one tutorial gave about 1.15 to 1.21 depending on the version, so the page shows 1.25 as a quoted historical value.

The Richardson plot is straight only over a limited range of scales and the dimension varies along a coast; the divider method also shows numerical artefacts even on the Koch island, whose dimension is known exactly.

inspirations: Mandelbrot's 'How long is the coast of Britain?'

design.coreLoop: Shrink the ruler, predict the next length, see it, then watch a chart point appear. The next rung asks the visitor to fit the line and read the slope; a check question confirms the idea before the next curve.
sophisticationHooks: A correct divider walk (compass steps along the curve, each step a circle-curve intersection) so the ruler really walks the coast rather than being faked
Live log-log chart with a draggable fit line and a printed slope and dimension, rounded to the precision the data supports
Seeded random coasts with hidden roughness for a guess-the-dimension round with the answer revealed by measurement
An honesty panel: real coasts are only roughly self-similar over a limited range of ruler sizes, and the model is exact only for the built curves
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: Koch, circle and seeded midpoint-displacement coasts generated in the browser, a divider-walk length function with unit tests, ruler slider, log-log chart with a draggable fit line, rungs 1 to 5, 4 check questions, explainer, and the quoted Britain figures as a static panel (rung 6). Cut: real map data, country comparisons, user-drawn coasts, any live data.
risks: Per-country dimensions (Australia, Norway, Portugal) came from one unreliable blog and are excluded; only the west-coast Britain 1.25 is shown, labelled as a quoted historical value.
The 50 km Britain figure differs between sources (3,400 versus 3,500 km), so the page says 'about' and shows the 3,400 figure as quoted, not measured here.
A course page gave the Koch dimension as 1.231; the formula ln4/ln3 = 1.2619 is used and the build should assert it in a test.

A divider walk on the built Koch coast gives a fitted slope that wobbles around the exact value (reported artefacts of the method): the build tests that the fit lands within a stated tolerance of 1 minus 1.2619 and the page says 'close to', never 'equal to'.
Plot convention: sources differ between plotting length (slope 1 minus D) and plotting step count (slope minus D); the page uses length and states the convention beside the chart.
Looks like a fractal-pretty-picture page: the lesson must keep the chart and the slope reading central.
The model is idealised: a real coast is not self-similar at every scale, and the page says so in its honesty panel.

verification.notes: No page could be opened (mathworld host already failed today); the Britain figures, Richardson's slope relation, the 1.25 value and the Koch numbers were each found in at least two separate results or follow from arithmetic.
